display: Freelance documentary editor in New York with an unfinished film of interviews with Chinatown elders.

signals.text: I have a documentary of interviews with Chinatown elders that has been stalled for years, and I want to get it moving again.
I need someone who can read Taishanese and tell it apart from Cantonese, so the interviews can be transcribed.
Three transcription services gave up on the Taishanese passages, or could not tell which parts were Taishanese and which were Cantonese.
A grant deadline is in March. I need a transcript, a 20-minute sample cut and a treatment, and the transcript is what is blocking the other two.
I'm looking for a grant writer or producer who has funded oral-history or immigrant-community documentaries.
I'm attending an online grant info session on 10 November and would like to hear from anyone who has applied to that program.
I'm deep in a client's rough cut, due 20 October. We disagree on whether the film should open on a person or on the dough.
I'm worried that waiting longer means losing more of the elders' stories. Two interviewees have already died.
I feel I owe the people I interviewed a finished film, and I haven't touched the drive in two years.
Money is tight. Freelance checks arrive about 60 days late.
I keep checking my email for a film fund decision and nothing has come.
I want to learn to keep a sourdough starter alive. Mine has died twice.
I'd like to find someone who can look at the old DVX100 and 5D footage and tell me whether it needs restoring or better audio cleanup.

offers.text: Fifteen years of documentary editing in Avid and Premiere. I have cut 31 films, two shortlisted at festivals.
Narrative structuring: I can turn a large pile of interview footage into a story with a clear arc.
I can build a sample cut or trailer for a grant application from raw interview material.
A network of grant writers, festival programmers and archivists, whom I can introduce when the fit is clear.
A small cut-room in a Gowanus studio, which I can use for review sessions.
English and working Cantonese. I understand Toisan but do not speak it.
About 60 hours of archival interviews with Chinatown elders, shot in 2015–2016 and digitised. I can discuss access terms for researchers or archives with the elders' families.
I can coach a youth baseball team and run practices for nine-year-olds.

catchers.hypo: I'm a linguist or graduate student who works on Taishanese. Do you have recordings that need transcribing, and would you pay for or share the work?
catchers.can: Share sample passages for a trial transcription, and discuss a paid or credited collaboration. The material stays private until the elders' families consent.
catchers.confirm: Can you transcribe spoken Taishanese yourself, as opposed to Cantonese or Mandarin?

catchers.hypo: My grandmother speaks Toisan and I can read Chinese. I'd like to help transcribe oral histories of the older generation.
catchers.can: Test one short clip and agree on a method, such as time-coded notes with a second reviewer, before committing to the full set.
catchers.confirm: Do you personally understand Taishanese when spoken, not only Cantonese?

catchers.hypo: I run a community archive or oral-history project in Chinatown. We're looking for stories from the older generation and for partners who can handle consent.
catchers.can: Talk through consent, access terms and a possible archive home for the interviews. I would introduce the right elders' families only with their permission.
catchers.confirm: Does your project handle consent from interviewees' families, including for people who have died?

catchers.hypo: I'm a grant writer who has funded documentaries about immigrant communities. I'd like to look at your treatment and timeline.
catchers.can: Share the treatment and sample-cut plan, and work backwards from the March deadline.
catchers.confirm: Have you written a successful application to a documentary fund?

catchers.hypo: I'm a small documentary producer. My editor dropped out three weeks before my rough cut is due.
catchers.can: Take on freelance editing if the schedule fits around school pickup, and say frankly whether the deadline is realistic.
catchers.confirm: Is this a project for broadcast, streaming or festivals rather than a short social-media edit?

catchers.hypo: My family has a laundry or restaurant story from the 1950s to the 80s. We have photos and tapes. Can you help us turn them into something?
catchers.can: Advise on structure and format, and maybe cut a short piece, depending on material and budget.
catchers.confirm: Do you have your own recordings, photos or footage, not only memories?

catchers.hypo: A relative of mine in Flushing is 80 and speaks Toisan. Could she help with a few passages of old recordings?
catchers.can: I would first ask my own family whether someone in the older generation is willing to help, and set up listening sessions only with consent.
catchers.confirm: Is your relative comfortable with this and willing to listen to the recordings in person?

catchers.hypo: I'm a parent of a nine-year-old in the league. Our team keeps losing and the kids sulk. Any suggestions?
catchers.can: Share what has worked for me: snacks after every game, laps for sulking, and keeping the focus on the team.
catchers.confirm: Do you coach or help with a youth team now?

forbids.text: I will not release any of the interviews without the consent of the elders' families.
I will not share the elders' names or addresses with anyone, whatever the reason.
I cannot take a full-time job, because I need to be flexible for school pickup.
I will not apply for a grant before I have a transcript of the interviews.
I will not pass off a machine transcript of the Taishanese passages as accurate without a human who speaks the language reviewing it.

projects.name: The Elders
projects.text: A documentary built on interviews with 42 Chinatown elders about their journeys and their work in laundries, restaurants and garment shops. It needs a transcript, a treatment and a sample cut before the March grant deadline.

policy.t1: When a collaboration looks promising, I will explain why the film stalled, what the transcription gap is, and which grant requirements I am working towards. I can share a few short, consented excerpts as test material.
policy.t2: Once I trust the other person and know who they are, I will talk about my money situation, my feelings about the interviewees who have died, and the project's real timeline.
policy.never: I will never give out the elders' names or addresses, or details about my family. I will not release any interview recording without the elders' families' consent.
